blocks.text: Chulin 63a, alongside the לקני (§. 227), the בטני is also named as a clean bird. The name (בטן) points to a thick- or broad-bellied bird, perhaps the gannet. The gannet too belongs to the pelican genus and is called Pelicanus bassanus, from the island of Bass, on which it multiplies greatly; perhaps, therefore, בטני may also have some affinity with bassanus; in any case, the pairing of לקני and בטני entitles us to think of the two birds of the related genus.
A Species of Gannet.

Chulin 93b it is said: The בטני (gannet §. 228) is permitted to be eaten, whereas the bird בטנאי is permitted to be eaten in some places and forbidden in some other places. Since the bird is not here declared absolutely unclean, one need only think of the difference between a more or less rigorous observance, and while some held the בטנאי, as a variety of the בטני, perhaps the sooty-brown species (Sula fusca), to be clean, others declared it unclean, as is the case with the various species of moorhen (§. 219).
The Bustard.

Chulin 63b, alongside בטנאי (§. 229), שקנאי is also mentioned; like the former, this bird too is eaten by some and not by others. We have already seen earlier (§. 201) שקי as a designation for the feet of birds, cf. also §. 202 and in addition the relevant Talmud passage, and so we also derive שקנאי from שק “shank,” by which the entire foot is designated. The bustard has long and strong feet, and may therefore have received its name שקנאי.

Some eat it because it resembles the turkey and is in general counted by some among the gallinaceous birds; others, however, on account of its thick, strong feet, placed it rather in the kinship of the aquiline birds. Cf. the cited Talmud passage.
The Wine-Drinker.

שהיא חמרא (Chulin 62b), which is forbidden to be eaten. The name points to a bird that eats the fruit of the vine, perhaps the redwing (Turdus iliacus), which is so called because it steals and eats grapes in the vineyards; it should be noted, however, that the common thrush (§. 262) is a clean bird, which incidentally still allows another bird of the same genus to be declared unclean, cf. §§. 219 and 229.
Perhaps here [p. 186] the vine lark (Alauda cristata) is meant; the common lark (§. 213) belongs to the eight birds doubtful with respect to cleanness
The Lapwing.

Chulin 62b the bird מונא חמרא (mixed wine) is forbidden to be eaten. Here one must doubtless think of a wine-coloured bird. In Aelian (Thierg. 4, 58) it is called Οἰνάς [Oinas]; it is smaller than the wood pigeon (Φάσσα [Phassa]) and larger than the common pigeon (Περιστερά [Peristera]), and is, as several explain it, the lapwing, French Vanneau. The bird may be so called because it is metallic dark green on the back, like the grape.
A Wine-Coloured Bird.

Chulin 62b it is said that the bird בת מונא חמרא (daughter of the מונא חמרא, see §. 232) is permitted to be eaten. In Aristotle (Naturg. 9, 36, 4) a bird is called Οἰνάνθη [Oinanthē], which some explain as a kind of wild pigeon, so called from the colour of the ripening grape. Indeed the stock dove (Columba oenas in L.) has a wine-red breast, and it is therefore rightly permitted to be eaten as a pigeon. Another species of wild pigeon is spoken of elsewhere (§. 255); yet it cannot be surprising that the various species of wild pigeon bore different names; the species mentioned here lives in holes in trees, the one to be mentioned later lives in clefts.
Two Species of Birds.

Chulin 62a it says: The bird מרדו זגיד ואכיל is permitted to be eaten, the bird סגיד ואכיל is forbidden to be eaten. Rashi reads מרה for מרדו, probably because מרדו is mentioned earlier (§. 219) as an unclean bird. Possibly one must here look for such birds as shake their head more or less; thus, as is well known, the starling runs with constant nodding of the head. The lexica [p. 187] do not even have the roots of those words, and perhaps a distinction must be made here between סגר “to bend down” and זגר “to raise.” But I do not venture to put forward any further conjectures.
The Linnet.

Chulin 62b the bird צרדא is declared a clean bird. Landau translates flax finch or linnet, since צרדא means flax. The linnet belongs to the sparrow genus and is therefore rightly permitted to be eaten.
The Snow Finch.

Chulin 62b the bird ברדא (Aruch reads: בר ארא) is declared an unclean bird. On this Landau remarks: “Perhaps it is the snow finch, which received this name not only from the white colour of the throat, the breast and the entire lower part, but also because it inhabits the cold lands. It is found in great numbers on the snowy mountains of the Caucasus and in Persia.”

But the snow finch belongs to the sparrow genus and should probably rather count as a clean bird, cf. §. 235. Why could one not think of the alpine chough, which belongs to the raven genus? I therefore leave the choice to further research.
The Sparrow.

Chulin 65a it says: The bird ציפרתי catches food in the air. Rashi says the ציפרתי is a clean bird; in general, according to the Talmud (ibid. 139b), צפור is in every case a clean species of bird. Although צפור is indeed a generic name, צפור is nevertheless probably, like the Latin Passer, in general the sparrow; in Hebrew as in Arabic the root word means to chirp, from which the sparrow has its name. The Latin word seems to be formed by transposition from צפר, while the German Sperling contains the Hebrew word in its first syllable.
The Hummingbird.
